title: Primitive Values and Immutability

content.explanation: Primitive values are the smallest indivisible values in JavaScript. There are seven primitive types: Number, String, Boolean, Undefined, Null, BigInt, and Symbol. These values are stored and copied by value, meaning each variable receives its own independent copy. One of the most important characteristics of primitives is immutability. Once a primitive value is created, it cannot be changed internally. For example, strings cannot be modified character by character. Instead, when a value appears to change, JavaScript creates a completely new value and updates the variable to point to it. Immutability improves predictability, simplifies memory management, and enables engine optimizations. Because primitive values never change after creation, JavaScript engines can compare them quickly and safely. Understanding primitive behavior helps explain why changing one primitive variable never affects another variable that was copied from it.
content.example: If let age = 25 and let newAge = age, changing newAge to 30 does not affect age because each variable has its own copy.
content.analogy: A photocopy of a document is independent. Writing on your copy does not change the original document.
content.keyTakeaway: Primitive values are immutable and copied independently by value.

revisionSummary: Primitives are immutable and copied by value.

mcqs.explanation: Strings are immutable and cannot be modified directly.
